( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** Even when one feels an extremely intense craving to eat meat, one’s desire should be satisfied by other means; animal slaughter is not appropriate. He says one should make <note>a substitute</note>. A "ghee-animal" <note>original: <term>ghṛtapaśuḥ</term></note> is a form made of clarified butter; because it resembles the form of animal meat, it is called an "animal." The same applies to an "animal" made of flour <note>original: <term>piṣṭapaśuḥ</term></note>. Regarding "attachment" <note>original: <term>saṅge</term></note>, it means a state of intense desire. Some say it refers to being overcome by spirits or similar forces, but that is not common usage, so the two reasons <note>craving or flour/ghee substitutes</note> are the intended meaning. ( 37 )

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** If there is attachment—that is, a passion for eating meat—one should make an image of an animal out of clarified butter or flour and eat that. One should never desire to kill animals without the purpose of offering to a deity. ( 37 )

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** An animal of clarified butter means an image of an animal made of ghee. "In attachment" refers to a situation where one is intent on animal sacrifice or has a passionate craving for food. This applies to mandatory domestic rituals <note>original: <term>smārta-karmāṇi</term></note>, but not to Vedic rituals <note>original: <term>vaidike karmaṇi</term></note>, because in Vedic rites, using a ghee-animal would contradict the rule of the eleven portions <note>an altar procedure requiring actual animal parts</note>. Therefore, it is said that "killing in a sacrifice is not killing." ( 37 )

( 5 ) **Nandana:** He explains that one should not perform slaughter against the rules. "In attachment" refers to a gathering for a festival or an assembly of kinsmen; in such cases, one should "bring near" <note>offer</note> a ghee-animal. In place of a real animal, one should give plenty of clarified butter and flour-cakes. ( 37 )

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** One should make a ghee-animal when there is attachment or desire. One should likewise make a flour-animal. One should never desire to kill an animal in vain <note>without ritual purpose</note>. ( 37 )

### As many hairs as there are on the animal’s body, so many times the one who kills an animal in vain will suffer a violent death in birth after birth in the afterlife. ( 38 )

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** He suffers a violent death for that many cycles of rebirth. A "vain animal-killer" <note>original: <term>vṛthā-paśughnaḥ</term></note> is one who performs animal slaughter that is not ordained by the Vedas or the Law-codes <note>original: <term>śruti-smṛtyoḥ</term></note>. This refers, in context, to hunters and others who kill for worldly purposes. The word "animal-killer" <note>original: <term>paśughna</term></note> is a Vedic grammatical form. ( 38 )

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** "So many times" refers to that specific number of times. A "vain animal-killer" is one who kills an animal not ordained by the Vedas or the Law-codes. ( 38 )

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** He who kills animals for his own sake, without the purpose of offering to a deity, is known as a "vain animal-killer." After death, he suffers a violent death for as many births as there are hairs on the animal's body. Therefore, one should not kill an animal in vain. The word "so many times" <note>original: <term>tāvat-kṛtvaḥ</term></note> uses a suffix to denote the repetition of an action. The particle "ha" here is used to indicate that this is well-known from the sacred tradition. ( 38 )

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** He states the penalty for the opposite case <note>wrongful killing</note>. The particle "ha" here highlights a well-known fact. ( 38 )

( 5 ) **Nandana:** "So many times" means that specific number of turns. The particle "ha" expresses compassion. ( 38 )

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** A man who is a "vain animal-killer," having performed a killing through unrighteousness in this world, attains the state of an animal in the afterlife for as many births as there are hairs on the animal—eighty million hairs. ( 38 )

### Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice, for the prosperity of this entire universe; therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing. ( 39 )

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** The previously mentioned fault does not apply here. Slaughter ordained by the Vedas and Law-codes as a part of a sacrifice is for the sake of bringing about prosperity. Animals were created—produced—by the Self-Existent One, Prajāpati. The phrase "himself" is an explanatory praise <note>original: <term>arthavāda</term></note>. "Of this entire universe" refers to the whole world, and "sacrifice" refers to rites like the Jyotiṣṭoma. "For prosperity" means for wealth, strength, and abundance. Therefore, the killing that occurs there is to be understood as "non-killing." This is said to indicate the absence of the sin that normally arises from violence. ( 39 )

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** He removes the doubt as to why such a fault does not exist in ritual killing. Sacrifice is for the "prosperity" of the world, meaning its birth; through the sequence of the offering reaching the Sun, which brings rain, which produces seeds, which leads to the production of semen, and finally the birth of living beings. By this, it is said that through the ritual slaughter of one animal, many living beings are sustained, and thus no such fault exists. ( 39 )

<summary>This page discusses the prohibition of "vain" animal slaughter and the ritual exceptions. It suggests using flour or ghee substitutes for meat cravings and explains the karmic penalty for non-ritual killing, while justifying sacrificial slaughter as a means for universal prosperity.</summary>
